original_question: For an integer m > 5, determine the smallest integer n such that every set of n points in space with no four coplanar contains m points lying on a common sphere. Ask the analogous question for other prescribed spatial figures such as cones or cubes, and for the planar version with m > 4 and no three points collinear.
target_in_paper: Unsolved Problem 9(a)–(c): determine the minimum n=n(m) forcing m of n points in space with no four coplanar to lie on the surface of a sphere, together with the analogous questions for an arbitrary spatial figure and for the plane. The paper is an informal problem list and does not contain a Conjecture 1.1, Proposition 1.2, or Theorem 1.3. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft is very close to the paper’s actual target. It correctly captures the threshold form of the question (“smallest/minimum n”), the hypothesis m>5 in space, the general-position condition that no four chosen points are coplanar, the conclusion that m points should lie on one sphere, and the two follow-up variants for other spatial figures and for the planar case with m>4 and no three collinear. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))
missing_details: The paper states the quantifier explicitly as “Find a minimum n (of course, n depends on m) having the property: no matter how one chooses n points…”, so a fully stand-alone version should make the universal quantification over all n-point sets explicit. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))

Part (a) says the m points “belong to a surface of a sphere”; your draft’s “lying on a common sphere” is close, but the paper’s wording emphasizes the sphere’s surface. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))

Part (b) is phrased for “an arbitrary spatial figure,” with “cone, cube, etc.” only as examples, so the rewrite should not narrow the paper’s scope to cones and cubes alone. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))

Part (c) is written only as “Similar problems in plane (for m > 4, and the points: three by three non-collinear),” so a stand-alone formulation must make the intended planar analogue explicit—namely, the circle analogue of part (a), and in parallel the analogue for prescribed planar figures. This clarification is an inference from the structure of Problem 9(a)–(c). ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))

The paper is informal and does not specify a coordinate field, normalization, or a formal model of “space” and “plane”; a faithful rewrite should therefore avoid adding extra geometric structure beyond ordinary plane/space language unless it is only a harmless clarification. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))

For part (b), the paper does not formalize whether one fixes a figure type in advance and asks for the corresponding extremal n, so the rewrite should phrase this as the analogous extremal question for a prescribed figure type rather than impose extra transformations or congruence language not present in the source. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))
refined_question: For each integer m>5, determine the minimum integer n=n(m) such that every set of n points in three-dimensional space with no four points coplanar contains an m-point subset lying on the surface of a common sphere. In the same sense, ask the analogous extremal question for an arbitrary prescribed spatial figure (for example, a cone or a cube); and ask the planar analogue for m>4, where one has n points in the plane with no three collinear and seeks m points lying on a common circle, and more generally on a prescribed planar figure. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))
justification: The draft matches Unsolved Problem 9 almost verbatim. Part (a) of the paper is exactly the sphere-forcing problem for m>5 in space under the “no four coplanar” condition; part (b) is exactly the analogue for arbitrary spatial figures such as cones and cubes; and part (c) is exactly the planar analogue for m>4 with no three collinear. Because this paper is a short, informal list of open problems rather than a developed article with theorem-style reformulations, the only sharpening needed is to make the universal quantifier and the implicit planar analogue fully explicit while staying close to the original wording. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))
